# Welcome {.unnumbered}

This book explains what happens to sequencing data **after you hand your
libraries to the sequencing core**. It is for people who make libraries at the
bench and want to understand, step by step, how their FASTQ files become
count tables, genome-browser tracks and QC reports. You don't need any
background in programming or bioinformatics: the Foundations part starts
from "what is a terminal?" and "what is a `.gz` file?".

The first module covers **bulk RNA-seq** using the lab's
[bagPipes](https://github.com/PhanstielLab/bagPipes) `RNApipe` workflow. Each
chapter takes one step (one Snakemake *rule*), explains what problem it
solves, shows the command bagPipes runs, and tells you how to judge whether it
worked. Later modules will cover **ATAC-seq** and
**ChIP-seq / CUT&Tag / CUT&RUN** in the same way.

::: {.callout-note}
**This is a curriculum, not a manual.** The [bagPipes
README](https://github.com/PhanstielLab/bagPipes) is the reference for running
the pipeline. This book explains the *why* behind each step, so the README and
the output files make sense. If the two ever disagree, trust the code in
`workflows/RNApipeCore.snakefile`.
:::

## What you will be able to do

By the end of the RNA-seq module you should be able to:

1. Use the shell to look inside any file in the pipeline, compressed or not,
   and say what each line and column means (FASTQ, FASTA, GTF, BED, bedGraph,
   bigWig, SAM/BAM).
2. Explain what each step is for, and name the common alternative tools
   (STAR vs HISAT2, Salmon vs kallisto, featureCounts) and what they assume.
3. Read a FastQC report and a MultiQC report and point out a problem.
4. Explain why reads are trimmed and what Trim Galore removes.
5. Describe the difference between **quantifying** reads against a
   transcriptome (Salmon) and **aligning** them to a genome (HISAT2), and say
   which output each one feeds.
6. Open a BAM file and a bigWig track in IGV and interpret what you see,
   including strand-specific tracks.
7. Fill in a samplesheet and config file, launch `RNApipe` on Longleaf, check
   on it, and recover from a failed run.
8. Load the results into R with `tximport` or `tximeta` and start a DESeq2
   analysis.
9. Explain how processing changes for nascent-RNA assays such as TT-seq.

## How to use this book

- **On your own:** read the chapters in order. Each one ends with a short
  *Check your understanding* box; the answers are folded underneath.
- **In a group:** the [Teaching guide](teaching-guide.qmd) splits the module
  into sessions with hands-on exercises on Longleaf.
- **As a reference:** the [Glossary](appendix/glossary.qmd),
  [Command cheat sheet](appendix/cheatsheet.qmd) and
  [Troubleshooting](appendix/troubleshooting.qmd) appendices are meant for
  looking things up.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Where does the data come from?

The exercises use the small test dataset that ships with bagPipes: four iMGL
RNA-seq libraries subsampled to 100,000 read pairs each, on Longleaf at
`/proj/phanstiel_lab/Data/processed/subsamples/rna/PE_100k/subsampled/`.
They run in minutes. If you want to practise on a published dataset, the
companion guide [download-public-data](https://jpflores-13.github.io/download-public-data)
shows how to pull FASTQ files from GEO/SRA with `fasterq-dump`.
:::

## Conventions

- `Code in this font` is something you type, a file name, or a program name.
- Blocks with a grey background are commands. Lines that start with `#` are
  comments and are ignored by the computer.
- `{sampleName}` in curly braces is a placeholder that Snakemake fills in,
  for example `IMGL_iMGL_WT_Ab_24h_1_1`.
- Tool versions quoted in this book come from `config/RNAconfig.yaml` in
  bagPipes (for example Salmon 1.10.3, HISAT2 2.2.1). Check your copy, because
  they change.
